purpose: Every important thought from the unsolved.md work, written the moment it is thought, so an agent that runs out of usage mid-task loses nothing. Append-only, newest last. Read THIS FILE FIRST on resume.

schema.at: ISO 8601 local time the entry was written
schema.by: agent that wrote it (fable-5.2, deepseek-v4.1-flash, argon, human)
schema.item: the construct or task, one line
schema.thought: what the writer is considering or has just realised - write it here the moment it occurs, before proving anything
schema.finding: what is actually true, in plain words
schema.evidence: reproduction path and the numbers that prove it, or null when it is still a thought

resume.build: export PATH=$HOME/.cargo/bin:$PATH; cd /tmp/rg-fable-wt && CARGO_TARGET_DIR=/tmp/rg-fable-target cargo build --release --target x86_64-unknown-linux-musl --features "deep parser"
resume.tests: CARGO_TARGET_DIR=/tmp/rg-fable-test cargo test  (then again with --features "deep parser")
resume.rule: Append an entry the moment a thought matters: which construct you are about to test and why, which reader you suspect, which file you are about to change, what the last measurement showed. kind=thought, status=thinking, no evidence yet - that is fine. Never batch to the end of a run: the account can cut you off at any tool call and anything not in this file or in a commit is lost. When a thought becomes a finding, append a new entry with the evidence and leave the thought where it is.

entries.item: js corpus is a random sample of every .js under both home trees
entries.finding: A large share of the js corpus was built output - webpack chunks, .next/static, dist, .min.js. Each is one enormous line, so per-line pairing has nothing to compare and its losses are noise no reader fix can remove. That is why js had been stuck at a low file count with high losses.
entries.evidence: old sample /tmp/opencode/sweep-local/js-minified-baseline: 96/1995 files, 164 losses. New source-only sample: 149/2000 files, 270 losses - fewer files pass because they contain constructs. Filter: /tmp/opencode/js-source-filter.py (>=15 lines, no line >400 chars, built dirs excluded); sweep-local.sh pipes through it.

entries.item: class field with a computed key: `static [entityKind] = "x"`
entries.finding: The lexer named the target `static` because unpack_targets only stripped const/let/var/my/our/local/val/mut; a class-field modifier is not a binding. The CST names the computed key, which is right.
entries.evidence: /tmp/js-static/a.js (4 lines): 1 loss -> 0. js 149/270 -> 138/244, ts 91/114 -> 84/107, python and rust held.

entries.item: rust method call after a block-like operand: `async { s }.boxed()`
entries.finding: After a block-like operand in statement position the grammar writes `.name(args)` as one field_expression carrying its own arguments, so no call_expression exists to read and the call left the record. Treating a field_expression with an arguments child as a call repairs it.
entries.evidence: src/deep_facts/rust.rs: rust_block_method + rust_call/rust_callee. Measured by deepseek-v4.1-flash in /tmp/rg-fable-wt: rust 260/1816 (287) -> 255/1816 (282); js, ts, python untouched.

entries.item: js for-header assignment emits an event the CST does not have
entries.finding: For `for (i = length; i-- !== 0;)` the lexer emits an `a` event with targets [i]; the CST emits nothing on that line because it records a for header's binder in the statement's target list. Suspect double accounting on the lexer side, but not yet confirmed against pipeline.rs.
entries.evidence: /tmp/js-for/a.js reproduces 2 losses (lines 17 and 32); the corpus shows 11 rows, but only about 2 distinct files.

entries.item: corpus duplication inflates every corpus, worst in rust
entries.finding: Measured by content hash: js 2000 files / 1854 unique (7% dup), ts 2000 / 1537 (23%), rust 1816 / 1000 (45%). The rust corpus is every .rs in the workspace, which now holds many near-identical worktrees, so almost half the rust losses are the same code counted again. Dedupe would reset every rust baseline - owner decision, not a lane decision.

entries.item: usage limit stopped the run mid-task
entries.finding: Fable 5.2 hit its 5-hour limit at 12:36 EST, resets 17:10 (America/New_York). It had applied the rust field_expression fix but not committed it. Its measurement helpers and reproductions are in /tmp/fable-m/tools and /tmp/fable-r.

The 2000-file js sample held 146 files that were byte-identical to another file in the sample (webpack copies of one library across build dirs). Every such file counted as its own fallback, so one construct moved the js number several times over.
entries.evidence: sha256 over the sample: 2000 files, 1854 unique. After dropping the duplicates the same binary reads js 125/1854 (223) instead of 138/2000 (244) - 13 files and 21 losses were pure duplicates. tools/js_source_filter.py now drops repeats by content hash during collection.

entries.item: ts `{} as Record<string, number>`: the type after `as` is not a value
entries.finding: `as` is already noise, so the lexer skipped the keyword but then read the type like an expression: the value of `const total = {} as Record<string, number>` came out as the type argument tuple, while the CST writes only the cast value `{}`.
entries.evidence: /tmp/ts-as/a.ts (4 lines): 2 losses -> 0 under both readers. Fixed by skipping the type expression after `as` in TS/TSX (Emit::skip_type: runs to the first token that cannot continue a type at depth zero). ts 84/2000 (107) -> 82/2000 (101); js, python and rust unchanged.

entries.item: ts declaration classes with multi-line type-parameter lists
entries.thought: 16 rows, all in declaration files (types.d.ts, index.ts declare class). A one-line signature in a class body is already suppressed, so the shape that breaks must be the type-parameter list that spans lines: `$$eval<` newline `Selector extends string,` newline `>(…): Promise<…>;`. The type parameters look like a group the statement never closes, so the class frame never opens and the members are read as module-level statements - my 2-file reproduction emits both signatures at `a.ts:<module>`. Cheapest next probe: check whether an unmatched `<` is what keeps the statement alive across those lines, before writing any rule.
entries.evidence: /tmp/ts-decl2/a.ts: 2 losses, both `no event on a line both readers can mean` at module level; /tmp/ts-c1 and /tmp/ts-c2 (one-line signatures, with and without `declare`) have 0 losses, so length is the trigger.

entries.item: js for-header events: extra lexer events are tolerated, so the 14 rows are pairing noise
entries.thought: /tmp/js-for3/a.js compares `for (i = 0; …)` against `for (var j = 0; …)`: the lexer emits an extra `x` (the condition merge) on both header lines and the CST emits neither, yet the file measures 0 losses. So a lone extra header event is not itself a loss - the corpus rows come from somewhere else (a line the CST attributes differently), and chasing them from the header side would be guessing. Leave this cluster alone until a reproduction shows a real disagreement.
entries.evidence: /tmp/js-for3: lexer x+body vs deep body on lines 3 and 4, losses 0. Corpus rows: 000399_index.js:82, 000995_natural.js:63/67/75, 001055_index.js:105.

entries.item: rust was skipping JavaScript and Python keywords as if they were its own
entries.finding: The generic NOISE list is a mix of JS, Python and Perl operators, and Rust went through it with only `new` excepted. So a Rust variable named `lambda`, `is`, `and`, `or`, `var`, `my`, `our`, `then`, `of`, `do` or `local` was skipped as if it were a keyword, and the value lost the name the CST writes (`self.line(lambda)` came out as a call whose argument was the constant 0).
entries.evidence: /tmp/rgn-lam/a.rs (7 lines): 1 loss -> 0. Fix: a Rust-only RS_NOISE list holding just the words that really are Rust keywords (await, yield, async, in, as, if, else, for, return, let, const, mut, ref, unsafe, pub, move). Measured: rust 255/1816 (282) -> 246/1816 (267); js, ts and python unchanged.

entries.item: ts nested type arguments with a comma break the statement, not the type parameters
entries.thought: Correction to my earlier note. A one-line generic signature is fine (`first<T>`, `first<T = unknown>`, `first<T extends unknown>` all measure 0 losses), and a multi-line type-parameter list without a nested comma is fine too. What breaks is a nested type argument carrying a COMMA: `first<T = Record<string, unknown>>(): Promise<T | null>;` inside `declare class D` emits at `<module>` instead of opening the class frame - one loss. So the trigger is the comma inside `<…>` being taken as a statement separator because the angle brackets are not bracket depth for the splitter. That is the thing to fix, and it is a general type-argument scanner, not a class-member rule.

entries.item: rust: a turbofish inside a call argument breaks the whole argument list
entries.thought: loss_shapes on all four corpora this hour: rust 267 over 244 files (223 empty-scope, then t: m:, m: m:, m: n:assert_eq 7 each), ts 101 over 64 (t: m: 16, t: n:never 7), js 223 over 125 (empty 42, then 0 8, m: m: 7, c(0; m: 7), python 18 over 14 (empty 5, n:Exception 2). The rust assert_eq rows all carry `Vec::<T>::new()` as an argument.
entries.finding: `assert_eq!(no_fill.iterate(), Vec::<MatchAction>::new())` loses the row: the lexer writes `m:[n:assert_eq,m:[c(n:no_fill;[0]),n:Vec,m:[n:new,0]]]` where the CST has `t:[c(n:no_fill;[]),c(n:Vec;[])]`. The turbofish skip in `chain` consumes `::<...>` but the callee the CST keeps for `Vec::<T>::new()` is `Vec`, and the argument list collapses (both args of side_tab_page merged into one `m`), so the failure is in the call-argument split around the turbofish, not in the chain. Repro: /tmp/rgn-turbo/a.rs, 1 loss.
entries.evidence: /tmp/rgn-turbo/a.rs 1 loss; got vs want in the entry above; 7 rows in the rust corpus (001162/001316 matching_core.rs:245, 001548 integrity_tests.rs:138/142/150, 001607 static_flush.rs:37, 001626 side_accent_radius.rs:124).

entries.item: ts: a defaulted type parameter closing as >> lost the class member's colon
entries.thought: The class frame was never the problem. `member_type_cut` counts `<` as depth and `>` as its closer, but the lexer emits `>>` as ONE op token, so `f<T = Record<string, unknown>>(): void` kept depth 2 at the colon, the cut was never found, and the member fell through to expression_event -- which is why the event carried the whole merged value.
entries.finding: Fix: `>>` and `>>>` decrement by 2 and 3 in member_type_cut. The four bracketing repros go to 0 losses (/tmp/ts-b1, /tmp/ts-m, /tmp/ts-m2, /tmp/ts-m3); ts 82/2000 (101) -> 80/2000 (89), js 125/223, python 14/18, rust 246/267 unchanged. Both cargo suites green.
entries.evidence: /tmp/ts-b1/a.ts 1 loss -> 0 with no flows at all (a signature writes nothing, which is what the CST does); tools/loss_count.py after the fix: ts 80/2000 (89).

entries.item: ts multi-line type parameter lists still emit at module level
entries.thought: /tmp/ts-decl2/a.ts still loses 1 after d0afd80: a member whose `<` opens at the end of one line and closes several lines later (`$$eval<` newline `Selector extends string,` ...). on_newline() only refuses to split when self.brackets is non-empty, and `<` never enters self.brackets. inside_type_arguments() already exists and is consulted by the comma rule, so the same guard belongs in on_newline -- but it must not swallow a real comparison (`a < b` at end of line), so it needs the `<` to be an opener in a declaration position, not any `<`.
entries.evidence: RG_LOSSES=1 on /tmp/ts-decl2 after the fix: 1 loss, 'event x line 3 ... wanted line 3 value t:[m:[n:$$eval,...'

entries.item: ts multi-line type parameter list: on_newline guard attempt failed
entries.thought: Tried the guard the note called for: in TS/TSX, do not end a statement at a newline when the line ends in `<` preceded by a name. Reverted.
entries.finding: The repro /tmp/ts-decl2 still loses 1 with the guard in place, so the split is not happening at the newline after `<`. The member is still emitted at module level, which means either the statement is closed elsewhere (the comma rules already skip inside_type_arguments) or the class frame is not the frame being used. Not worth a second guess without a debug build; the next attempt should instrument the statement boundary rather than pattern-match.
entries.evidence: built with the guard (2m24s), /tmp/ts-decl2 losses=1 (unchanged), /tmp/ts-b1 and /tmp/ts-m still 0. Patch reverted with git checkout.

entries.item: js: the deep reader writes a constant for an identifier named async
entries.thought: loss_shapes on js put `c(n:env.stack;[m:[m:[n:value,n:value],...` at 7 rows: `env.stack.push({ value: value, dispose: dispose, async: async })`. I first patched expr.rs (the lexer's object-pair path) to collapse `k: k` shorthand - that made the LEXER wrong for all pairs and I reverted it (`git checkout`). The flows show the lexer is right and the deep reader is wrong.
entries.finding: /tmp/js-obj2 isolates it: `f({async: async})` is the only failing shape (`{x: async}`, `{async: 1}`, `{async}`, `{yield: yield}` all pass). --lexer writes `m:[n:async]`, --deep writes `0`. So the deep reader's value rendering treats an identifier named `async` as a keyword and emits the constant, in an object property value position. Fix belongs in deep_facts (go.rs value rendering), not in expr.rs.
entries.evidence: /tmp/js-obj2/{a,b,c,d,e}.js: only a.js loses 1. Flows: --lexer a.js:f [['x',2,['c',0,['n','env.stack'],[['m',[['n','value'],['n','dispose'],['n','async']]]]]]] vs --deep [['m',[['m',[['n','value'],['n','value']]],['m',[['n','dispose'],['n','dispose']]],0]]]. Corpus rows: 7 (000249_Frame.js:55 first).
